headline: This law extends a limited antitrust exemption for colleges that admit students without regard to ability to pay, and it removes one way those colleges could share financial data.
what_it_does: Colleges that admit all students on a need-blind basis can make agreements with each other about how they give need-based financial aid without breaking antitrust law. The extension runs through fiscal year 2022. The law also ends a permission that let these colleges share, through an independent third party, financial data a student or family submitted before aid was awarded. That sharing was allowed only if each college could get the data just once for each student.

who_it_affects.group: Colleges and universities that admit all students on a need-blind basis
who_it_affects.how: They keep an antitrust exemption that lets them coordinate how they administer need-based aid, but they can no longer share applicant financial data through an independent third party in the same way.

who_it_affects.group: Students and families applying for need-based financial aid
who_it_affects.how: Financial information they submit may be shared among colleges through a different route than before, or not at all, depending on how each school handles aid data.

who_it_affects.group: Financial institutions that submit financial data on behalf of families
who_it_affects.how: They are no longer covered by the permitted third-party data exchange that applied to data they submitted for aid applicants.

when_it_takes_effect: The law took effect when it was enacted on August 6, 2015. The antitrust exemption it extends lasts through fiscal year 2022.
